utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-R77.2, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My name is Bruce MacFarlane. I'm an attorney from Canada appearing as the amicus curiae prosecutor in these proceedings, and with me is Lori Ann Wanlin, also from Canada. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. MacFarlane and Ms. Wanlin. Good morning, Mr. Seselj, you may be the first accused to have two status conferences in a row at the same courtroom changing the Trial Chamber. And if you could state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dr. Vojislav Seselj, university professor, and the most accused individual by The Hague Tribunal. And I'm representing myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that you are following this procedure in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The decision on allegation of content and the order in lieu of an indictment were issued on 21st of January this year. The indictment charges the accused, Mr. Vojislav Seselj with one count of contempt of the Tribunal for knowingly and willfully interfering with the administration of justice by disclosing confidential information in violation of orders granting protective measures in a book authored by him. On 11th of February in year, Mr. Bruce MacFarlane, Queens Counsel, was appointed as amicus curiae prosecutor in this case by the acting Registrar, and the Initial Appearance of the accused was held on 6th of May, 2009, where the accused pleaded not guilty. That said -- 6th of March. Thank you. That said, there's one thing I would like to raise with the accused, which is to inform him that the name, the title of the book, remains confidential in order to avoid the danger of the identity of the protected witness being revealed. So, I tell you, Mr. Seselj, in clear language not to name or reveal the title of the book during the course of Status Conference or procedure in public session. The Chamber, this Chamber has convened this Status Conference to deal with any preliminary issues before starting a trial and hear any issues to raise from the parties. Until yesterday, this morning, there was only one outstanding motion pending before the Chamber pertaining to the disclosure. However, thanks to the decision issued this morning, filed this morning by the Trial Chamber III, most of the issues have been resolved, I take it. I wonder whether Mr. MacFarlane has received the decision of the Trial Chamber III?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I have not yet received it. I've been in meetings all morning and I didn't realise a decision had been issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My information is that the Chamber has allowed access to all the transcript and relevant records of the case thereby resolving most of the issues you raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I look forward to reviewing that decision immediately upon completion of this Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is wondering if, to expedite things, if you are handed over the decision right now and given, say, about 20 minutes, whether you can deal with the issues later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I fully expect that I will be able to do that with about 20 minutes. Perhaps even less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, would I be correct in assuming that with your Canadian heritage that you'll be able to read the decision which is in French?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Between my colleague and I, with our Canadian background and heritage, we'll be able to work our way through the decision, but I'm grateful for the advance advice in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether Mr. Seselj can read the decision in French, but we will make sure that decision should be disclosed to you as well. We'll rise for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Our hearing is resumed. Mr. MacFarlane, having seen that decision of the Trial Chamber III and the response, the response from the OTP, I wonder whether there are remaining issues on your part to pursue further?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At the outset I'd like to thank the Registry, not only have we reviewed the transcript but we now have possession of all the materials referred to in the order that was arranged during the course of the recess, so I'm very grateful for that. I believe that this meets the request and the needs of the Prosecution. The only qualification that I would add is that under the heading "Ordonne," in the second paragraph there is a reference to the OTP forwarding materials to -- perhaps through the Registry to the amicus, and on reviewing that material, there may well be further questions and there might be further avenues. I won't know that until I receive the materials from the Office of the Prosecutor. But subject to that perhaps minor caveat, it appears that I have the materials that I'll need to move forward in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the Chamber didn't have enough time to study the decision by the Trial Chamber III in full either, but let's move forward on that basis. I will turn to briefly on disclosure issues. On 27th of April, the Trial Chamber ordered the ex parte status of supporting materials, and I take it that those materials have been disclosed to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there any issue relating to translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes. There are -- continue to be a number of issues relating to translation. There's a couple of points I'd like to make, Your Honours. The assignment in this case actually has three components to it. One relates to the preparation of the trial. The second involves an investigative component because there was no investigation prior to the order in lieu of indictment. And the third involves the redactions referred to in the decision of this Trial Chamber. The translation issue arises in each of those three components. We are working our way through the issues. And in terms of disclosure, disclosure is complete, there's one final document which is being provided to the accused today, and it involves a chart concerning the publication in question, the book. And this chart is a combination of both English and B/C/S. The B/C/S will allow the accused to trace through his own book so that the portions relating to his book are in English, but it allows him to understand where he needs to go to in his own book, so it was felt it was unnecessary to translate that part. That is being provided to the accused today through the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What issues alive are there in relation to investigation referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The investigation largely involves acquisition of the documents and reviewing the documents and assessing whether or not there's further documents that are necessary. With the order of today, we will be able to move forward in a more complete way on that front, so I would expect that we'll be well positioned to complete the investigation. But that's -- in essence the nature of the investigation is the review of the initial material that was provided and then assessing what further documents or statements or materials were needed and then if they are covered by an order of confidentiality, taking the appropriate steps to obtain them. So that's been the nature of the investigation thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I meant to come to this issue later on, but how do you see the issues in this case? What issues there are alive in relation with respect to this indictment, as you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: In terms of the indictment and the Prosecution component of the three that I was referring to earlier, the main issues that we are looking at the moment involve an analysis of the manner in which confidential information was disclosed and the linkages that are sprinkled throughout the book and that involved a fair bit of work because the translation -- an independent translation was necessary. I say independent, independent of the Office of the Prosecutor. So that's the -- been the bulk of our work is to obtain the translations and then try to piece together what is in essence a jigsaw puzzle of references, and it's been quite challenging. We are working our way through that, but that was necessary in order to understand whether and at what point and in what way protected witnesses were identified. It's in essence one large jigsaw puzzle that we are now putting together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, the indictment, Mr. MacFarlane, says that the book contains numerous references to witnesses. It gives their pseudonyms and then says "including their real names, occupations and places of residence, which enable the identification of these witnesses." Are you suggesting that's an oversimplification of what seems a very straightforward allegation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's oversimplification or not, I don't believe it is, but the book is 1400 pages in length, the electronic book, and the direction was to carry the Prosecution independently, and we've done that, so our reliance upon OTP analysis has not been necessary. But the task of putting together all of the various pieces with a view to understanding when and under what circumstances and where the disclosures were made has been a time-consuming process. It's in part a function of the fact that the book is a very lengthy one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am afraid I'm not understanding this. Either there are clear statements of the identity of these protected witnesses in a book published under the name of the accused or there are not. And if there are, what else is it that the Prosecution would intend to prove other than the circumstances in which the accused came to know that the material was confidential?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think that there's -- I could put it in this way, there's really two points that need to be made. First of all, there's -- this is not a book where there's simply a stand-alone passage which identifies protected witness by a name and puts everything together in -- even in one page. The book has to be looked at as a whole. And that's been -- that's been the challenge is going through the entire book because there are various references at various points and unless you can link all of those references together, sometimes you don't know that the reference is being made to a protected witness. As an example, in some instances a -- well, it's probably unnecessary to go into illustrations in open proceedings, but suffice it to say that one has to take a look at the book as a whole in order to understand how all the various pieces link together. And secondly, second point I wanted to raise was that a very important component in understanding whether and under what circumstances the accused revealed confidential information we had to obtain the statements. And that has just been provided to us today. So that will allow us to complete the investigative task and get ready for trial. But those are two important factors in understanding the nature of the investigation and the preparation for trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me please, are you saying that the book has been translated so far as necessary or has not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I made arrangements to retain the services of an expert translator who has gone through every line and every paragraph and every page of the book. He provided advice on those portions of the book that potentially identified either directly or indirectly, and then once that advice was received, we have been making arrangements for a formal translation by staff translators within the Tribunal. So in that sense, the book has been completely reviewed. We have not arranged for a written translation of the entire book. That was thought to be impractical. We are arranging to have the relevant portions of the book translated. The vast majority of what has been identified has been translated. We just obtained what is probably either the last or the penultimate group of pages that we need yesterday, yesterday. So certainly the vast majority of the pages that require translation has been done. There might be some residual pages, they won't be many in numbers but we are very close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there's a disclosure issue here as well because the English translations would have to be disclosed to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: That's an issue that we'll -- we'll have to consider because the translations relate to the very publication of the accused, so the chart that's been provided today makes that link. It in essence says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you need to give him the English version. That's all I'm saying. I appreciate that you can link it and don't necessarily need to do certain things, but whatever is going to be available in English will have to be disclosed to him. So you'll have to hang your colours to the mast pretty quickly on that front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The -- I appreciate the issue that's been raised by the Chamber. The accused's position, as I understand it, is that he wants all disclosure in B/C/S. So we kind of go around in a bit of a circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but this is a situation where we are dealing with something in B/C/S that the Chamber has to understand in English, and the accused is entitled to have it in English. What he does with it is entirely a matter for him. But he plainly is entitled to it and it would not be surprising if issues over the translation actually arose in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I appreciate the comments of the Chamber and I will give them very, very careful consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll give you the floor very soon, Mr. Seselj. Could you wait a minute. Mr. MacFarlane, I take it that you didn't understand our indictment and order in lieu of indictment to mean that you should investigate all the contents of the book and identify any other passages which reveal the identity of the protected witness and include them in the charges or propose the redaction of those parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I guess that there's really two separate issues here. One is the trial, and the order in lieu of indictment. The other was what I'll refer to as the redaction project. And certainly on the redaction side, it was my understanding that the Chamber was seeking advice on those areas of the book that ought to be redacted and we've proceeded on that basis starting with page 1 straight through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber meant only those pages referred to in the indictment, in the decision should be examined by the amicus. That was our Chamber's understanding. That said, Mr. Seselj, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it should be very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you try again. Could you repeat, start again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For any serious lawyers, it must be extremely surprising that first indictment is issued and then it is followed by investigations. It should have been done in reverse order. Investigations should have come first and the result of the investigation would be an indictment. First we have the indictment and then we have an amicus curiae who initiated investigation after the fact. This raises the question about how to conduct these proceedings. Since all the charges here are based on a book, it requires for the entire book to be translated. One cannot use only excerpts from a book. You cannot extract a quote from a book unless you present the entirety of the book. I'm not quite sure that the Prosecutor is fully aware of the structure of the book. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (redacted). This part of the book, as a public document, was submitted to the Trial Chamber with the objection to indictment number 3. I'm not quite sure but it's not important. This particular document that has 300 pages -- okay, you are not interested maybe in this so I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you are going to refer to the content of the book or speak in the way the title of the book can be revealed to the public, we'll go into private session. So your reference to the place will be redacted and if you could bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not going to mention either the name of any protected witnesses or the title of the book, and I guarantee that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This passage will be redacted as well. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You may as well redact everything. I was just trying to be helpful with the structure of the book. Since you don't need my help, I'm not going to deal with that any longer and I will leave it to your own devices, you and the OTP to deal with that. In addition to my first objection that the indictment preceded the investigation and that the whole book has to be translated in order to be a subject of the proceedings, I would like to say one more thing and that is that the disclosure of supporting documents, according to Rule 66(i), has not been done completely. According to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, this should have been done one month after an entering of plea. This has been disclosed to me only partially. According to the Rule 66(i), I was entitled to disclosure of all documents. It also provides the possibility for a number of documents not to be disclosed but clearly reasons why this can be done are stipulated therein. Since all the documents supporting the indictment have not been disclosed to me, primarily the request by the OTP, which still remains ex parte, and some of the appendices to this request such as document 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8, et cetera, that is to say, I still don't know what am I going to defend myself fully against. And for that reason I'm not going to raise any objections to the indictment or the order in lieu of this indictment. The OTP failed to do this within the time-limit for various reasons, and one of the reasons is that you as the Trial Chamber maintained the position of the OTP that some of these documents should remain ex parte and for that reason I'm not going to object to this indictment. I have been denied the possibility to use these documents in the proceedings and this will only give you time, extra time for you to institute the proceedings at an earlier date. This is what I had to say at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber made it sure to -- that all the relevant material, relevant for this case, be disclosed to you as supporting material. And my understanding is that has been done. The other materials referred to, in my understanding, have nothing to do with this case, and that's totally separate -- related to a separate matter. So that resolves the supporting -- disclosure of supporting material. And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May be allowed to say one more thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that all the material mentioned here must have something to do with these proceedings and the case because why else would it be attached to the request made by the Prosecutor. So that is a justified assumption on my part, that everything that is there has to do with this case. Now you are telling me that everything that is ex parte does not have anything to do with this case. Now, if that is the case, why should it be here at all under the ex parte status? There's no reason for it to be contained there. Why should it be ex parte at all? Why wasn't it just thrown out of the case? There's no logic there. On the one hand, it is in this case and has the status of ex parte, and you all know what it is, you the Judges know, the Prosecutor knows, I am the only one who doesn't know. And on the other hand, you tell me those are matters which have nothing to do with this case. So there's no logic as far as I'm concerned there. And that's why I'd like to ask you to explain that to me. Why would it be included in the case if it has nothing to do with the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All I can say, Mr. Seselj, at this moment, those materials have nothing to do with this case and we'll proceed with this case. That's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you want me to believe you at your word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will make sure every relevant material be disclosed to the accused. As for the translation, Mr. MacFarlane, you commented that most of the translation has been done. That's good news. Do you -- as for the 66(a)(ii) disclosure, do you intend to call any witnesses for the purpose of prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to answer that. I need to take a look at the material that was -- that will be provided to me and has been provided to me this afternoon. I'll make an assessment after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is minded to start this trial pretty soon and given that, how much time do you think you need to prepare all these?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Given the fact that we now have the materials that we were seeking, I believe that we could proceed to be ready for trial with dispatch and I would expect that we would be in a position to proceed in the latter part of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber's preference is to hold the trial as soon as possible, i.e., in late May, this month. And to that end, the Chamber would like you to file a 65 ter list, witness list, if any, as well as exhibit list in a week's time, by the end of next week, and indicate to the Chamber whether the amicus prosecutor is up to start the trial as early as late May. Now, do you have anything to say, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, simply to indicate that I will certainly follow the direction of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I turn to Mr. Seselj. If I can ask the same question put to the Prosecution, i.e., what issues do you see in this case on your part?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already told you the problems that I have. The problem of disclosure first because some material has been proclaimed ex parte material. I have no other problems. I'm trial-ready as of tomorrow. I'm ready to go to trial straightaway. I plan to call five witnesses, but I might give up on them. If the Prosecution doesn't call witnesses, then I might not call any witnesses either. If we are just going to discuss the book. I'm ready to go to trial straightaway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sometimes a Chamber asks the parties whether there is any agreed fact or not, but we have transcript reference in which you admitted that authoring the book, so do you admit that you authored that book in question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only do I accept the fact that I am the author of the book, I'm very proud of being the author of that book, and it is thanks to these legal proceedings that there is a lot of interest in the book. On my internet site several thousand copies have been photocopied and reproduced, so I'm very satisfied. I'm very satisfied to have been the author of that book. So that is an indubitable fact. That's how things stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Seselj. I think I exhausted all the agenda I noted down but whether there are any -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was about to ask whether there's any issues on your part to raise, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just one issue. Reference has been made to preparation of witness lists and exhibit list but there's no reference to a pre-trial brief. Was the Chamber going to provide any direction in that respect or is the pre-trial brief essentially waived in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The rules are applied mutatis mutandis to the contempt proceedings, so I wonder whether that's necessary in this case. I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that it is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you have anything to raise with the Chamber? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to repeat my request to be allowed to sit up front in the first row, which is the Defence counsel's position, and as I'm defending myself, it's very important that visually I be on par and have equal status as the Prosecutor in the courtroom. And I've already made that request, I told Mr. Parker that at my Initial Appearance. So as the Trial Chamber, it is up to you to rule on that request. Because you know as judges how important it is that both sides in the proceeding are not only on a footing of equality generally speaking but visually too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber noted your request made at the previous Status Conference, as well as the ruling Judge Parker made at the time and we do not defer from that position, i.e., the Chamber finds no reason to depart from the general practice of this Tribunal. That said, we'll rise and then after having received and seen the 65 ter lists, the parties will be notified as to the date of trial in due course.
